text:
That explains hallucination. The model writes plausible continuations, and a plausible continuation of a question is an answer. Whether a real answer exists isn't something it can check. The capital of France is... Paris. It's seen that millions of times. A twenty nineteen study on this by... Chen et al. found a twenty-three percent improvement. Just as fluent, and that study was never in its data. It's read millions of citations, so it nails the shape: names, a year, a journal. But nothing marks a fact as, I actually know this one.

The risk isn't spread evenly, though. It climbs when the fact is rare, specific, or made of several parts, when it's past the training cutoff... and when the question assumes there's an answer. The capital of France scores zero out of five. The name of the study that proved this? Four.

[curious] So why not just say, tell me if you don't know? You'll get more hedges... but they don't land on the wrong answers, because nothing inside knows which ones are wrong. What works is changing the task. Paste in the source. Ask for something you can check. Constrain the shape. And give it an exit, like, reply not found. It's picking a continuation either way, so hand it an easy, honest one. Pasting in the source means filling the context window. And the window has limits of its own.

The context window is everything the model reads in one request: the system prompt, the documents, the history, the question... and the answer it writes, all from one budget. In a two hundred thousand token window, one long document leaves just six thousand three hundred tokens to answer in. And past the edge, nothing fades. It's simply not there. Apps quietly trim old turns to fit, which is how a long chat forgets its own beginning.
